ms.promise:
Tx building code and tests.
The spec outlines what types of txs should be build-able. These make up the transitions of the subbit channel lifecycle for "typical txs" (as opposed to exotic txs where the user wishes to also include conditions legal yet irrelevant to subbit, eg split an output value between 2 different addresses). The tx building code is an implementation of this part of the spec. 
Tests will provide some coverage of successful txs, as well as failing txs. It (clearly) will not be exhaustive.

ms.promise:
SDK, and a How-To guide on wrapping an existing service with Subbit.xyz
M2 Tx building outputs components of managing a subbit channel. 
M3 extends M2 output with a set of functions and/or services that facilitate the integration of subbit ie a subbit SDK. 
**An appropriate form this takes is not yet known.**
Both client and server (ie consumer and provider) require persistent state including signing keys, and an l1 interface for monitoring channels as well as building and submitting txs. There is not a one-size-fits-all answer to this since it depends on the execution context for each. 
We presume that the client and server interact via http requests (although the core of subbit is agnostic to transport. Snail mail would also work). Perhaps subbit can act as "middleware" both sides leaving the application otherwise untouched. However it is likely that for only the most basic applications (eg where the cost of a request can be deduced by regex on the url) will the application and costings be so decoupled. 
The term "SDK" is, on reflection, suboptimal. There is no compiler, which according to various blogs is a typical part of what forms an SDK. However, neither "API" nor "library"

ms.promise:
Orcfax integration: payment solution based on Subbit
Orcfax is an oracle service provider for the cardano blockchain. Orcfax clients are typically dapps. They request oracle data, aka fact statements, to be made available on the Cardano blockchain. 
Typically the relationship reflects that appropriate to Subbit: there is a consumer and a provider in which the consumer is repeatedly making small requests of service over a period of time. 
The output is real world application using subbit. 
A client can:
* view channel state and manage channel (ie open, fund, close, drain).
* place orders for fact statements
* see historical orders.
A provider can:
* view subscriber channels
* handle orders.
It is likely the output has components that are web based guis, although we reserve the option to use a cli based interface if its deemed more appropriate.
Clients will likely wish to place orders programmatically as well as manually. The output should address this.
ms.criteria:
* A requirements document that reflects on Orcfax clients reported needs (particularly wrt integrating the orcfax payment solution with their product and programmatic orders) 
* Other high level design documents including a component diagram, ER or similar 
* The app handles the required feature set outlined above. 
* Early iteration has been used by beta users with feedback given.

ms.promise:
Open sourcing the Orcfax integration as a real world application.
This is not just: change repo setting, git add OS license. 
Open sourcing includes that, but is really about making the code accessible to any interested party. 
The readme will outline the overall repo layout, and the pre-req dependencies (eg `node + vite`), and the key commands for building, testing and running (eg `pnpm i && pnpm test && pnpm server`). 
It will also contain an explanation of expected resources and how to acquire/ run them (eg blockfrost key, ogmios/kupo) and signposting to where a user can find out more about these. 
The output includes a blog post-esque piece that introduces and tours the code. 
The piece contains reflects on the design decisions made (in place of any more formal ADR) and comments on possible alternatives and extensions.

* Repo has a standard open source license, contributing guidelines, and changelog (which initially may be empty).
